title: The road to gold: training and peaking characteristics in the year prior to a gold medal endurance performance
authors: Tonnessen E, Sylta O, Haugen T, Hem E, Svendsen I, Seiler S
population: 11 Olympic and World Champion cross-country skiers and biathletes (4 men aged 28 +/- 1 y, VO2max 85 +/- 5 mL/min/kg; 7 women aged 25 +/- 4 y, VO2max 73 +/- 3). Not runners.
findings: The 11 athletes reported one year of day-to-day training before the best competition of their career: about 800 h and 500 sessions a year, about 500 h of it sport-specific, 94% aerobic endurance training.
Of the aerobic training about 90% was low intensity (below the first lactate threshold) and 10% high intensity by time; 23% of sessions were classed as high-intensity sessions.

Volume and specificity followed a traditional periodization model, but the absolute volume of high-intensity training stayed stable across phases, and its pattern tended to become more polarized in the competition phase.
Training volume, frequency and intensity were unchanged from the pre-peaking to the peaking period; volume fell 32 +/- 15% (P < 0.01) from the preparation period to the peaking phase.
The athletes did not follow tapering practice derived from short-term experimental studies: only 3 of 11 took a rest day in the last 5 days before the competition.
limitations: Eleven elite skiers and biathletes, a different sport from running, with training reported after the fact for one year by the athletes. Descriptive: no comparison group and no outcome other than the best competition itself. Volumes (about 800 h a year) are far above those of a recreational runner. Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: A description of what elite endurance athletes did in the weeks before a best performance: volume, frequency and intensity held, the absolute amount of hard work held across phases, and the fall in volume coming between preparation and peaking. It is consistent with holding a plateau until the taper and with not raising the amount of hard work inside it.
It is not a test of holding, in another sport, and it gives no number of weeks for a plateau or a level for it; it does not support a higher weekly peak for a recreational runner.
